title: HTML Heading Elements
summary: Introduces the h1–h6 heading elements, the difference between a tag and an element, and why headings describe a page's hierarchy. Ends with an exercise that turns a flat line of text into a book outline using h1–h4.

concepts.heading: Tags vs elements
points:
A tag is anything wrapped in angle brackets.

is the opening tag;

is the closing tag. The only difference between them is the forward slash after the <.

An element is the whole unit: opening tag + content + closing tag. So

Hello World

is one h1 element whose content is the text 'Hello World'.
The two terms get used loosely online, but the distinction matters when reading docs: 'tag' means the markup, 'element' means the thing in the page.

concepts.heading: What headings are for: hierarchy, not size
points: The idea is borrowed from a book's table of contents: a top-level title, chapters under it, sections under chapters, sub-sections under sections.
HTML gives exactly six levels: h1 (most important) to h6 (least). There is no h7. Anything below h6 in importance should use a different element (paragraphs etc., covered later).
Browsers style headings by default so h1 is the largest and h6 the smallest. That default styling is only a visual hint of the level; CSS can change the look later without changing the meaning.

is invalid. Each level uses the same number in both tags.

concepts.heading: Heading best practices (conventions, not errors)
points: Use only one h1 per page. Think of it as the book title. Every other heading goes underneath it as h2, h3, and so on.
Don't skip levels. If a page has an h3, it should also have an h2 above it. Go h1 → h2 → h3 in order as you need deeper levels.
Breaking these rules won't break the page visually. They're professional conventions, and they matter for accessibility and search engines, which read the heading outline.

concepts.heading: Workflow introduced in this lecture
points: Download the lesson's starting files from the Udemy 'Resources' button (zip named after the lesson, e.g. '2.1 Heading Element').

Unzip/extract the download first, then move the extracted folder into a single 'Web Development Projects' folder kept somewhere permanent. Unextracted zips are the most common reason the folder won't open properly in VS Code on Windows.
In VS Code: File → New Window → open the Web Development Projects folder in the Explorer.
Each exercise folder has index.html (where you write code), solution.html (check only after attempting), and a goal image showing the target result.
Preview with the Live Preview extension: right-click index.html → Show Preview. If it's missing, the VS Code setup lessons were skipped.
Saving (Cmd/Ctrl+S) may auto-format the file and change indentation. That's normal and doesn't affect the result.
MDN Web Docs is the reference to check whenever you meet an unfamiliar element. Don't read it cover to cover; look things up as you need them.

task.name: 2.1 Heading Element: book outline
task.starting_point: index.html contains the words Book, Chapter 1–3, Section 1/2 and Diagram 1 as plain text. In the preview they run together on one unformatted line with no hierarchy.
task.goal: Mark up the text with heading elements so the preview matches the goal image: a clear book → chapter → section → diagram outline.
steps: Wrap 'Book' in a single h1 (the page title).
Wrap each 'Section N' inside the chapters in h3.
Wrap 'Diagram 1', which belongs to Section 1 of Chapter 2, in h4. It's the deepest level used.
Save, check Live Preview against the goal image, then compare with solution.html.
task.expected_result: Four visibly different heading sizes in the order h1, h2, h3, (h4), with one h1 and no skipped levels.
